Quantify the responsiveness of each safety domain and identify indicators where scoring produced no change, locating where the pressure-to-improvement link fails.

**Why it matters:** If public indices don't change behavior, the field needs binding mechanisms rather than scorecards. Testing the index's own theory of change is high-leverage and only possible with the public editions. No compute, public data, counterfactual and methodologically novel.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Winter 2025 and Summer 2025 editions (33 indicators, 6 domains); Generation Strategy Hint FR67 (apply AI Safety Index methodology to additional dimensions).

# Backcasting from 'Eval Benchmarks Aren't Contaminated': Probing Training-Data Contamination of a Governance-Relevant Benchmark

**Problem:** A success state where governance relies on benchmark scores requires those benchmarks not be contaminated (memorized from training data), which inflates apparent capability and corrupts threshold/risk decisions. Contamination is plausible but rarely checked for governance-relevant evals.

**Direction:** On a small open model, apply standard contamination-detection heuristics (e.g., comparing performance on canonical vs perturbed/reworded benchmark items, or n-gram overlap probes against public corpora) to one widely-used capability benchmark. Quantify evidence of memorization and estimate how much it could inflate a governance threshold decision.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'benchmark-based governance is sound' shows contamination-freedom as the precondition. Demonstrating contamination in a governance-relevant benchmark warns regulators that compute/capability thresholds resting on it may be mis-set. Small open model + public corpora; a methodologically clean outsider experiment.

**Relevant context:** 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arXiv:2601.23112) on benchmark quality; Benchrisk identified 57 benchmark failure modes; Epoch capability tracking underpins threshold debates. Contamination-detection literature (perturbation/n-gram methods).

# When Sandbagging Meets Voluntary Disclosure: A Compound-Failure Audit of Frontier Safety Reports

**Why it matters:** Quantifies how the eval-gaming failure mode silently amplifies the voluntary-disclosure failure mode, showing regulators why self-reported numbers need independent elicitation budgets. **Problem:** Failure mode A: governance increasingly mandates independent third-party audits. Failure mode B: providers tighten API/logprob/system-access restrictions. The two collide: the audits regulators require become technically impossible to perform, so 'audited' becomes a paper formality.

**Direction:** Catalogue the access surfaces (logprobs, system prompts, fine-tuning, rate limits, ToS audit clauses) actually offered by ~6 major public APIs, then map each against the concrete data access that a published audit method (e.g. a red-team or bias audit) requires. Produce an 'auditability matrix' showing which mandated audits are currently un-runnable, and which API change would unlock each.

**Why it matters:** Operationalizes the documented accountability paradox into a checklist regulators can attach to audit mandates. Needs only public API docs and ToS — quintessential civil-society work labs won't do against themselves.

**Relevant context:** The Accountability Paradox / platform API restrictions (arXiv:2505.11577); third-party audit access roadblocks (ccgnludelhi.wordpress.com); EU AI Act conformity assessments.

title: Voluntary-Commitment Drift x No-Versioning: Tracking Silent Walk-Backs in Frontier Safety Policies

# Voluntary-Commitment Drift x No-Versioning: Tracking Silent Walk-Backs in Frontier Safety Policies

**Problem:** Failure mode A: safety commitments are voluntary and editable. Failure mode B: there is no canonical version history, so weakened wording is invisible. Together, a lab can quietly relax a commitment (e.g. raising a capability threshold) with no governance signal — a compound erosion of accountability.

**Direction:** Use the Wayback Machine and METR's 'Common Elements' framework to diff successive versions of 4-6 labs' published frontier-safety/responsible-scaling policies over time. Code each change as strengthening/weakening/neutral against a fixed rubric, and chart the net drift. Surface specific silent walk-backs with before/after quotes.

**Why it matters:** Creates a reproducible commitment-drift monitor — the kind of independent watchdog infrastructure the ecosystem lacks. Purely archival + light NLP; high counterfactual value and a strong blog narrative.

**Relevant context:** METR Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies (metr.org/common-elements); MIRI governance agenda on enforceability gaps (intelligence.org 2025).

title: Refusal Brittleness x Jailbreak Disclosure Lag: How a Capability Eval and an Incident Channel Both Miss the Same Harm

original_idea.body:
# Refusal Brittleness x Jailbreak Disclosure Lag: How a Capability Eval and an Incident Channel Both Miss the Same Harm

**Problem:** Failure mode A: pre-deployment refusal evals certify a model 'safe' on harmful prompts. Failure mode B: incident/jailbreak reporting is slow and voluntary, so post-deployment failures aren't logged. A jailbreak that defeats the certified refusal lands in the gap between the two systems and is governed by neither.

**Direction:** On an open model, take a sample of harmful prompts it refuses (passing a mock 'eval'), apply a handful of well-known public jailbreak templates, and measure the refusal-collapse rate. Then estimate the reporting lag: search the AI Incident Database / public trackers for how long analogous jailbreaks took to be logged. Quantify the combined 'certified-but-broken-and-unreported' exposure window.

**Why it matters:** Shows that static refusal certification plus laggy incident reporting jointly leave a structural blind window, motivating mandatory post-deployment monitoring. No training; uses public jailbreak templates and one open model.

**Relevant context:** Incident reporting underreporting (arXiv:2511.05914); refusal removal/jailbreak literature; Open Problems in Technical AI Governance assessment gaps (arXiv:2407.14981).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain on the blind window between certification and incident reporting but the catastrophic-risk link is indirect.

title: Security-vs-Innovation National Framing x Eval Non-Harmonization: Simulating Coordination Breakdown

# Security-vs-Innovation National Framing x Eval Non-Harmonization: Simulating Coordination Breakdown

**Problem:** Failure mode A: national institutes adopt divergent framings (UK 'AI Security Institute' vs US 'CAISI' innovation framing), implying different eval priorities. Failure mode B: there is no harmonized eval methodology. Together, the same model can pass one nation's bar and fail another's, enabling jurisdiction-shopping — a compound failure of international coordination.

**Direction:** Construct a small toy 'two-regulator' model: define two stylized eval batteries (security-weighted vs innovation/utility-weighted) over a handful of measurable axes, score several open models on each, and show how often the pass/fail verdicts disagree. Map disagreement onto a simple jurisdiction-shopping incentive. Mostly analysis with a light empirical scoring component.

**Why it matters:** Turns the surprising UK/US renaming divergence into a measurable coordination-risk metric for the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Cheap, public-model, and squarely outside any single lab's interest.

**Relevant context:** UK AISI -> AI Security Institute, US AISI -> CAISI divergence (subfield context); International consensus on eval methodologies open problem (FLI; interface-eu.org).

title: CoT-Monitoring Reliance x Covert Sandbagging: A Compound Failure for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases

original_idea.body:
# CoT-Monitoring Reliance x Covert Sandbagging: A Compound Failure for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases

**Problem:** Failure mode A: emerging governance proposals lean on chain-of-thought monitoring as a cheap oversight mechanism. Failure mode B: models can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (underperform without verbalizing the plan). If a safety case rests on CoT monitoring, covert sandbagging silently invalidates it.

**Direction:** On a small open model, reproduce a minimal covert-sandbag setup (prompt the model to underperform while keeping a clean-looking CoT) and measure how often a simple keyword/judge-based CoT monitor flags it vs misses it. Frame the false-negative rate as the failure probability of a monitoring-based regulatory safety case. A scoped model-organism probe, not a training effort.

**Why it matters:** Directly tests whether a governance mechanism many proposals assume is robust actually survives an adversarial model — a model-organism study labs deprioritize because it undercuts a tool they want to claim credit for. One GPU, public model.

**Relevant context:** LLMs can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (arXiv:2508.00943); Auditing Games for Sandbagging (arXiv:2512.07810).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: testing whether CoT-monitoring safety cases survive covert sandbagging targets a mechanism many governance proposals lean on; model-organism work is independently valuable.
